title: Harvesting worm castings from a vermicomposter
subtitle: Getting finished castings out without losing too many worms, and putting them to best use
excerpt: Worm castings are the most nutrient-dense compost a kitchen produces. Harvesting them from a stacking wormery or a flow-through bin requires separating the worms from finished material. The separation method matters: rush it and you lose half the working population; do it well and the worms repopulate within a fortnight.
sourceNotes: RHS guidance on vermicomposting; Bentley Christie, Worm Farming Secrets (red wigglers and casting harvesting); Mary Appelhof, Worms Eat My Garbage (2nd edition).

glossaryTerms.definition: The solid excretions of compost worms — a finished, fine-textured compost with a higher available nutrient content than standard compost and a rich microbial community.
The liquid that drains from a wormery or compost bin. In vermicomposting, sometimes called 'worm tea', though true worm tea is made by steeping castings in water rather than using raw drainage.

content.text: Worm castings look like fine dark crumble — no visible food scraps, no smell beyond damp earth. When the bottom tray of a stacking wormery is 90% castings and few worms remain in it, it is ready to harvest. Rushing this step and scooping from an active tray takes the worms with the castings.
Knowing when the castings are ready
The tray is full of dark, earthy, fine-textured
When you open the tray, most worms have migrated up to the active feeding tray above. A few worms in the lower tray are normal; large numbers mean the tray has not finished processing.
A stacking wormery typically produces one harvestable tray every 3–4 months for a 2-person household with regular kitchen waste input.
Move the castings tray to a well-lit area — on a table near a window, in daylight. Spread the contents into a wide, shallow pyramid on a piece of card or newspaper.
Wait 15 minutes. Red wigglers avoid light; they migrate down and toward the centre of the pile.
Gently scrape the outer, top layers of castings off the surface into a container. The worms remain in the centre base of the pile.
Repeat: reform the pile from the remaining material, wait 10 minutes, scrape the outer layer. Two or three cycles separates most of the castings with minimal worm loss.
Return the worms (in the remaining small ball of material) to the active wormery tray.
Seed-raising compost: mix 1 part castings to 3–4 parts peat-free compost. Castings are too rich to use undiluted for seedlings — excess available nitrogen causes lush but fragile growth.
Potting compost top-dressing: a 10–20 mm layer worked into the surface of a container.
Liquid feed: steep 1 part castings in 10 parts water for 24 hours, stir, strain, and apply to plant roots. The
collected from the wormery sump is a ready-made version of this, diluted 10:1 before use.

rows.symptom: Many worms still in the bottom tray after 3 months
rows.cause: Bottom tray has not finished processing; too much fresh or wet material still present
rows.fix: Stop adding food to the bottom tray for 2–3 weeks; place food only in the tray above. The worms will migrate up as the bottom tray exhausts.

rows.symptom: Castings smell sour or like silage
rows.cause: Tray too wet; anaerobic conditions developed in the lower section
rows.fix: Mix in some dry shredded cardboard; leave the lid off for a day to allow air circulation. If the smell is strong, delay harvest by 2–3 weeks.
